Battle of Chancellorsville. From April thirtieth to May sixth, eighteen sixty-three, Robert E. Lee achieved what many considered his greatest tactical masterpiece. Despite being outnumbered two to one, he defeated Union General Joseph "Fighting Joe" Hooker's Army of the Potomac in the dense Virginia woods known as the Wilderness. Lee boldly split his forces, sending Thomas J. Jackson on a daring flanking march that surprised and routed the Union right. Yet this Confederate tactical victory came at a devastating cost—the loss of Jackson, Lee's most trusted lieutenant. And Lee's failure to exploit the victory prevented the capture of the Union army.

Hooker commanded the Union forces after Burnside and sought to exploit Lee's smaller force through rapid maneuvering. He planned to send cavalry around Lee's left while his main army crossed the Rappahannock to flank the Confederate position. Lee, informed of Union movements, correctly divined Hooker's intent and took aggressive action.

Lee divided his force, leaving ten thousand troops under Jubal Early to face Union frontal attacks at Fredricksburg. Jackson meanwhile marched approximately twenty-eight thousand troops on a twelve-mile route around the Union right, arriving on May second to attack the exposed flank. Union forces were routed. Hooker, despite his numerical superiority, lost confidence and began withdrawing toward his starting position.

But victory turned to tragedy. Jackson was wounded by friendly fire on the evening of May second and died on May tenth. Lee said simply, "I have lost my right arm." Lee pursued and attacked again on May third and fourth, but he could not force decisive victory. Hooker withdrew across the Rappahannock. Union casualties were approximately seventeen thousand. Confederate casualties were thirteen thousand. Though smaller in number, these losses were less replaceable for the South.

Chancellorsville was the apex of Lee's offensive genius—a maneuver of almost reckless audacity that worked because Lee understood his enemy and his subordinates' capabilities. Yet Jackson's death exposed a crucial vulnerability in Confederate strategy. The Confederacy lacked trained officers capable of replacing Lee's vision. Without Jackson, Lee's subsequent campaigns, including Gettysburg, would lack the coordinated execution they required.
